title: EnumSet & EnumMap: Extreme Performance Collections
summary: Discover why EnumSet and EnumMap drastically outperform HashSet and HashMap: explore 64-bit long bitmask vectors in RegularEnumSet, direct ordinal array indexing in EnumMap, zero collision overhead, and production state machine designs.
learningObjectives: Explain the internal bit-vector representation of RegularEnumSet (single 64-bit long primitive) and JumboEnumSet (long[])
Analyze how EnumMap achieves O(1) direct array indexing via enum ordinal() without hash computation or bucket collisions

Construct specialized EnumSet instances using noneOf(), allOf(), of(), range(), and complementOf()
Architect high-throughput permission systems and finite state machines utilizing EnumSet and EnumMap
expectedOutcomes: Replace slow HashSet/HashMap instances with EnumSet/EnumMap whenever keys or elements belong to an enum type
Execute ultra-fast bitwise set algebra (unions, intersections, complements) at CPU instruction speed
Guarantee deterministic key iteration order matching enum declaration order without sorted collection overhead

activities.title: Practical Context: Rotary Telephone Switch vs Telephone Directory Lookup
activities.description: Why fixed-domain lookups are orders of magnitude faster than generic hash hashing.
activities.content:
Imagine locating an employee's desk. In a city of 10 million people, you must consult a massive global directory, compute a district hash, traverse streets, and handle name collisions—this is `HashMap` and `HashSet`.

Now imagine an aircraft cockpit with a fixed panel of 12 circuit switches. The flight engineer doesn't consult an alphabetical directory to flip the landing gear switch; each switch has an immutable hardware index (0 to 11). Checking whether all hydraulic systems are active requires inspecting a single 16-bit register in one clock cycle.

`EnumSet` and `EnumMap` are the hardware cockpit: because the entire universe of keys is fixed and numbered at compile-time (via `ordinal()`), Java bypasses hashing, linked nodes, tree bins, and memory pointers entirely, operating directly on CPU bitmasks and contiguous array slots.

activities.title: Bit-Vector and Ordinal Indexing Mechanics
activities.description: Under the hood of RegularEnumSet, JumboEnumSet, and EnumMap flat array memory architectures.
activities.content:
### Formal Computer Science Definition
`EnumSet` is a specialized high-performance `Set` implementation for use with enum types, representing set membership as a compact bit-vector. `EnumMap` is an array-backed `Map` whose keys are enum constants, mapping each key directly to its array offset via `key.ordinal()`.

### Bitmask Mechanics of `EnumSet`

`EnumSet` is an abstract class that instantiates one of two private concrete subclasses based on the enum's universe size:
1. **`RegularEnumSet`** (universe size $\le 64$ elements):
   - Backed by a **single primitive `long elements`** (64 bits).
   - Membership test: `(elements & (1L << e.ordinal())) != 0`.
   - Insertion: `elements |= (1L << e.ordinal())`.
   - Removal: `elements &= ~(1L << e.ordinal())`.
   - **Performance**: Every basic set operation compiles down to single CPU bitwise operations (`AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `NOT`) executing in a single clock cycle.
2. **`JumboEnumSet`** (universe size $> 64$ elements):
   - Backed by a `long[] elements` array, where word index is `e.ordinal() >>> 6` and bit offset is `e.ordinal() & 63`.

```
                      RegularEnumSet (64-bit primitive long)
Bit Index:   63 62 ... 5   4   3   2   1   0
            +---+---+ ... +---+---+---+---+---+
Value:      | 0 | 0 | ... | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 |  --> Represents {READ, WRITE, EXECUTE}
            +---+---+ ... +---+---+---+---+---+
                           ^       ^   ^
                           |       |   +-- ORDINAL 1: READ
                           |       +------ ORDINAL 2: WRITE
                           +-------------- ORDINAL 4: EXECUTE
```

### Internal Architecture of `EnumMap`
Unlike `HashMap`, which allocates an array of `Node<K, V>` references with hash codes, linked lists, and tree nodes, `EnumMap` allocates:
- A private array `Object[] vals` of exact length matching `keyUniverse.length`.
- Lookup: `vals[key.ordinal()]` ($O(1)$ guaranteed, zero hashing, zero collisions, zero branch mispredictions).
- Space overhead is negligible: exactly one reference per potential enum constant.
- Iteration order is strictly the enum's declaration order (`ordinal` 0 to $N-1$).

### Structural Comparison Matrix

| Attribute | `HashSet` / `HashMap` | `EnumSet` / `EnumMap` |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Underlying Storage** | Hash table with linked buckets / red-black trees | Primitive `long` bitmask (`EnumSet`) / flat `Object[]` (`EnumMap`) |
| **Time Complexity** | $O(1)$ average, $O(N)$ or $O(\log N)$ worst | Guaranteed $O(1)$ single-cycle bitwise / array dereference |
| **Memory Allocation** | ~32 bytes per node + table array resizing overhead | Single 64-bit primitive or tight array (zero extra nodes) |
| **Cache Locality** | Poor (pointer chasing across heap nodes) | Exceptional (contiguous CPU L1 cache locality) |
| **Null Support** | Allows 1 null key | Strictly forbids `null` keys/elements (throws NPE) |

questions.question: How does RegularEnumSet store membership for an enum with 16 constants?
options: In an array of 16 boolean flags
In a single 64-bit primitive long bitmask where each bit index corresponds to an enum ordinal
In a balanced binary search tree indexed by name
questions.explanation: RegularEnumSet uses a single primitive long field ('long elements'). Because the enum has 16 constants, each constant maps to bit (1L << ordinal()), requiring no heap node allocation.

questions.question: Why does EnumMap guarantee zero hash collision and deterministic O(1) performance?
options: Because it runs an MD5 cryptographic hash on enum names
Because keys are mapped directly to array offsets using their fixed ordinal() integers
Because it dynamically resizes its capacity when collisions occur
Because it uses spinlocks to serialize key hashing
questions.explanation: Every enum constant has a unique, dense, zero-based integer index returned by ordinal(). EnumMap directly indexes an internal Object[] array with key.ordinal(), completely bypassing hashing and collision resolution.

questions.question: What is the iteration order of keys in an EnumMap?
options: Natural declaration order of the enum constants in source code
questions.explanation: EnumMap iterations traverse the internal array from index 0 to length - 1, which guarantees traversal in the exact order the enum constants were declared.

questions.question: Why should high-frequency trading and low-latency financial systems strictly replace HashSet<Enum> with EnumSet?
questions.answer:
HashSet<Enum> incurs significant CPU and memory penalties: it creates a HashMap.Node object for every entry, runs hashCode() and equals() checks, and accesses memory via pointer chasing across random heap locations, triggering CPU L1/L2 cache misses.

In contrast, EnumSet (RegularEnumSet) represents all members within a single primitive long. Set containment, union, and intersection compile directly to single CPU instructions (AND, OR, NOT). Furthermore, it produces zero heap allocations during containment checks and fits entirely inside a single CPU register, delivering microsecond-level latency improvements.

questions.question: How does EnumSet handle enums that define more than 64 constants?
questions.answer: When an enum exceeds 64 constants, EnumSet.noneOf() or of() automatically instantiates JumboEnumSet instead of RegularEnumSet. JumboEnumSet is backed by a 'long[] elements' array, where each element is a 64-bit word. The bit position is calculated as wordIndex = ordinal >>> 6 and bitOffset = ordinal & 63. While slightly slower than a single long, it remains drastically faster and more compact than HashSet.

practiceProblems.title: Bitmask Permission Checker
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given `enum Privilege { READ, WRITE, EXECUTE, DELETE }`, implement `boolean hasAllPrivileges(EnumSet<Privilege> userPrivileges, EnumSet<Privilege> requiredPrivileges)` that returns `true` if `userPrivileges` contains every privilege present in `requiredPrivileges`.

practiceProblems.title: EnumMap Inventory Counter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given `enum Severity { LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL }`, implement `EnumMap<Severity, Integer> countSeverities(Severity[] alerts)` that tallies the occurrences of each `Severity` present in `alerts`. Missing severities should not be in the map (or have count 0). If `alerts` is null or empty, return an empty `EnumMap`.

practiceProblems.title: Complementary Access Filter
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given `enum Role { GUEST, USER, MODERATOR, ADMIN, ROOT }`, implement `EnumSet<Role> findRestrictedRoles(EnumSet<Role> grantedRoles)` that returns an `EnumSet` containing all roles from `Role` that have NOT been granted, using `EnumSet.complementOf()`.

practiceProblems.title: Sequential Level Range Selector
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given `enum Level { TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL }`, implement `EnumSet<Level> getActiveLevels(Level minLevel)` that returns an `EnumSet` containing all levels from `minLevel` up to `Level.FATAL` inclusive, using `EnumSet.range()`.
